Experimental work on the globally abundant cyclopoid copepod Oithona similis has clarified key life-history parameters under controlled thermal conditions. In laboratory cultures held at a stable temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], newly hatched nauplii possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ grams [Wwb = approximately 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ grams], a value derived from the species' mean egg diameter of 57 μm. This minute initial mass, equivalent to about 0.097 micrograms, reflects the yolk-limited endowment typical of small pelagic copepods. From this starting point, individuals undergo a period of rapid somatic growth through six naupliar and five copepodite stages, with body carbon content increasing from a mere 18.0 nanograms at birth (18.0 ng)  to a substantially larger adult carbon mass. The ability to rear this species through its complete life cycle in the laboratory has enabled precise quantification of these growth metrics, which are essential for understanding population dynamics and secondary production in marine ecosystems where O. similis often dominates the mesozooplankton community.

Further ontogenetic investigations, all conducted at the same controlled temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], reveal that sexual maturation in Oithona similis is achieved after a relatively brief developmental interval. The time since birth at puberty, marking the point at which gonadal differentiation is complete and individuals become capable of mating, is approximately 20.0 days [tp = approximately 20.0 days] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This accelerated pace of development, from a freshly hatched nauplius to a functional adult, is characteristic of small-bodied copepod species that exploit productive environments and typically exhibit high population turnover. By the time females reach this pubertal stage, their body carbon content has climbed to 550.0 nanograms (550.0 ng) , an increase of more than thirty-fold from the carbon mass at birth. This value also represents the ultimate carbon weight attained by adult individuals in the species (550.0 ng) , as growth in body size effectively ceases once the pubertal molt has been completed and the terminal adult instar is reached.

Reproductive output in Oithona similis has been characterized in detail through laboratory rearing experiments. At an experimental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum reproduction rate is realized under optimal food conditions, with females producing up to 37.4 eggs over a 23.8-day period. This translates into a mean daily egg production of roughly 1.57 eggs per female, though the maximum recorded daily rate reaches 2.5 eggs per female [Ri = daily rate reaches 2.5 eggs per female]. Fecundity in this species is relatively modest compared to larger calanoids, but the continuous, low-level spawning strategy is well-suited to the oligotrophic environments O. similis frequently inhabits. The 20.0-day interval from birth to pubertal maturity (20.0 days) [tp = 20.0 days] means that females begin contributing eggs to the population within their third week of life, while the extended lifespan allows for repeated bouts of egg production over many subsequent weeks under favorable conditions at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

Longevity in Oithona similis has been assessed in sustained laboratory cultures maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], revealing a maximum lifespan of 45.0 days [am = 45.0 days]. This duration, spanning approximately six to seven weeks from hatching to natural death, is typical of small, rapidly reproducing planktonic copepods and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early maturation and continuous reproductive effort over extended somatic maintenance. The 45-day lifespan encompasses the 20-day pre-pubertal growth phase followed by approximately 25 days of adult reproductive activity, during which females can produce multiple clutches. This schedule places O. similis among the shorter-lived members of the Oithonidae, yet its high fecundity and rapid generation time facilitate population persistence in seasonally variable environments where windows of food availability may be brief. Post-reproductive senescence, characterized by reduced feeding activity and gradual physiological decline, typically occupies the final few days of life.

Comparatively, the life-history traits of Oithona similis align closely with expectations for a small-bodied, broadcast-spawning cyclopoid copepod operating at temperate water temperatures. The transition from a wet weight at birth of 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ grams [Wwb = 9.7 × 10⁻⁸ grams] to an adult carbon content of 550.0 nanograms (550.0 ng)  represents a substantial but achievable increase given the 20-day pre-pubertal growth phase (20.0 days) [tp = 20.0 days] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The consistency between the carbon weight at puberty and the ultimate carbon weight (550.0 ng)  underscores the deterministic nature of growth in this species, where body size is fixed upon reaching the adult molt. When viewed alongside the maximum lifespan of 45.0 days [am = 45.0 days] and a maximum daily egg production of 2.5 eggs [Ri = daily egg production of 2.5 eggs], all quantified at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], these values paint a coherent picture of a species adapted for rapid population increase during brief productive seasons, a strategy that underpins its numerical dominance in many coastal and oceanic zooplankton communities worldwide.
